summary: The US trade chief says a Canada deal is "fairly close", all five Ontario education unions now hold strike mandates, and Ottawa and Ontario put $928 million into Ford's Oakville plant.
body: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Sunday that the US and Canada are "fairly close" to a trade deal and that there has been "a lot of progress".[^1][^2] Talks restarted this month after collapsing in August. Greer also raised "concern" about Canada letting in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles a year at a low tariff.[^1][^2] Canada's chief negotiator, Janice Charette, has said several issues are still open, above all the 25% US tariff on Canadian cars, which is set to rise to 50% in January.[^1][^2] For Ontario, where many jobs depend on the auto industry, this is the key number to watch.

All five of Ontario's main education unions, covering teachers and support staff, have now voted 94 to 98 per cent for strike mandates. A mandate gives a union the right to strike later; it does not mean a strike is coming. Several legal steps, including conciliation and a 17-day countdown, come first, and one union leader called job action before Christmas "highly unlikely".[^3] Education Minister Paul Calandra says there is "absolutely no imminent strike threat". Unions say they want smaller classes and more help for students with special needs and mental-health needs.[^3]

On Nov 20 Ottawa and Ontario each pledged about $464 million toward a nearly $5 billion project at Ford's Oakville plant, which will be retooled to build heavy-duty pickup trucks for export. The federal government says it will protect more than 2,000 jobs.[^4] Industry Minister Mélanie Joly also said Stellantis owes the government "hundreds of millions" for not restarting production in Brampton.[^5]
This week: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem speaks in Toronto on Tuesday about the economy, ahead of the Dec 9 rate decision, and Statistics Canada publishes third-quarter GDP on Nov 30.[^6][^7]
differences: On trade, Greer sounds upbeat, while Canada's negotiator stresses the issues still unresolved.[^1][^2] On schools, unions describe years of cuts, while the minister says there is plenty of time to reach a deal.[^3]
